title: The Three Afflictions by Which the Proprium's Claim Is Undone
reading:
The proprium suffers three bitter afflictions, three contests, three dangers — and the source of all of them is the light. Wherever divine truth begins to shine into the natural mind, the soul's self-claiming feels it as a wound, because every degree of recognition is a degree in which the claim is loosened from what it had taken as its own.

The first affliction comes at the very outset. What the proprium sends forth from itself to dominate the natural — its own particular self-loving arrangements — turns and reigns over it. The forms by which it tried to rule become the bond that holds it in place. It is taken from the midst, separated from what it thought was its possession, and bound within the living principle that the Lord has set at the center. This is the first contest: the soul discovers that what it claimed was claiming it back, and that the very life by which its proprium operates is not its own.

The second affliction is the time of loosening, sorting, and dividing in the great fire of love. Whatever the proprium had hidden within itself — every interior good and truth it had taken as its own and shut away inside its claim — is shaken out and gathered inward to its proper place. What was always the Lord's is restored to the order it had at the first, before the soul ever claimed it. This is felt by self-love as destruction, because what is being undone is precisely the structure by which it kept what was not its own; but what is actually happening is the return of every concealed good to the arrangement it held from the beginning.

The third affliction is the final separation, when every thing is discriminated. The active form of self-love — the proprium in its asserting strength — is gathered into its own settled mass and sealed there. The receptive form of self-love — the proprium in its inward holding — is brought inward to its tomb. Between them, fixed forever, stands the firmness of what cannot be moved. The proprium's fruit comes to its own heaven, heavy and bitter, where there is no further unbinding: it is split, divided, and separated from the soul forever. What the soul had claimed is at last set apart from the soul, and the long mingling is over.
